## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

whys.g1: Both answers say the person who signs off was waiting on another office (the DA, the neighbouring sheriff) before deciding, and "Another office's view comes first" says that plainly, the way a chief would put it.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; both are straight answers about who has to agree.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The two answers say different things — one would pay more once a pilot proves faster reports through review, the other won't spend taxpayer money on work officers are already paid to do — so leaving each on its own is right, and there is no group either should have been put in.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; both are real answers about price.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, idea, then who pays, which suits how I sell, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) sits apart from the first-step screens (20–21), where a free pilot is already my answer, so it reads like a late afterthought.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20–21 (the first real step, which for me is a free pilot with a few officers) and screen 22 (Offer a pilot?) cover the same decision; screens 3 and 4 also carry the identical context question.
founder.missing: The chief's spending cap: whether the yearly total for the department ($6,000–$8,000) stays under what the chief can sign without the council. That threshold is why we win against Axon's ~$30,000 Draft One, and the per-officer price alone does not capture it. Also, whether the prosecutor's office will accept AI-drafted reports, which can stop adoption even after a chief buys.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The side-by-side trial against Axon's tool (screen 6) comes before the free pilot question (screen 7), and it assumes I already run Axon's tool and have decided to buy, when the pilot would naturally come first.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 both ask, in effect, whether and how I'd trial it with officers before committing.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether we already use Axon Draft One or another report-writing tool and our RMS, how many officers we have, CJIS compliance and data security, and whether our prosecutor and courts would accept AI-drafted reports.

screens.why3: I know my price, $30 per officer a month, so I can answer this from what I actually charge.
screens.why4: "A percent of the incident reports" is nonsense for police report software, "a percent of what it gets back" fits debt recovery, not a department, and per-officer pricing, which is how agencies buy, only shows up in the locked words.
screens.why5: The belief line, "Police chiefs would think it worth $30 per officer a month", is exactly my price and my buyer, with per officer and a month kept.
screens.instead: What price do you have in mind for something that cuts the paperwork after a call? — A fee per officer each month / A flat fee each year for the department / A fee per report / One price, then a yearly fee / Free to them; chip: No price yet

screens.why1: Right after who decides and the price, it is obvious to ask who else has to sign off before the chief can buy.
screens.why2: Chief, council and city manager are the plain words of my trade, and the hint that "Nobody" is an answer reads at once.
screens.why3: I know who signs off on department purchases from Heber City's chief and the spending cap, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: A free-text box with a "Nobody" hint and a leave-it-out chip covers every true answer, and the escape fits.
screens.why5: My point is that under the chief's spending cap nobody else signs, and the council or city manager only come in above it; the belief keeps the 'nobody else' but drops the cap, so it sits oddly beside the council and manager I typed.
screens.instead: Below the chief's spending limit, who else has to agree before the department buys? ("Nobody" is an answer; say who signs above the limit too.)

screens.why1: Right after I named who else might have to agree, it makes sense to show the roles back and let me check them before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The officer and chief rows say what each does, but the city council and city manager rows have no tag, so I have to read twice to see whether Keel thinks they sign off or are just listed.
screens.why3: I know who buys in a 10-to-200-officer department: the chief signs within the cap, and the council or city manager only come in above it.
screens.why4: The four roles are the right ones, but two rows are unlabelled and 'patrol officer' and 'Police chief' are capitalised differently, which makes the list look half-finished.
screens.why5: The belief 'the chief decides, nobody else has to agree' is what I said, but listing council and manager as 'people involved' with no tag blurs that they are only the alternatives I want tested.
screens.instead: The people involved: patrol officer · has the problem; police chief · decides to buy (within the spending cap); city council · only if above the cap; city manager · only if they sign software contracts

screens.why1: It follows straight from my last answer listing the council and the city manager, and asks which of those beliefs I want tested, so I see why it is here.
screens.why2: The options are plain, but 'Pick the one role; nothing is reworded here' is Keel's own housekeeping talk and makes me read the intro twice.
screens.why3: I know how chiefs buy: under the cap the chief signs alone, above it the council has to agree, so I can pick without guessing.
screens.why4: The three choices are the right ones from my list, but 'Nobody else' sits oddly under 'pick the one role', and the box's placeholder 'the one you pick had to agree' reads wrong for it until the real bar appears.
screens.why5: Picking 'Nobody else' gives 'The police chief decides, and nobody else has to agree', which is exactly my Heber City under-the-cap reading.
screens.instead: Which do you want to test? — The chief decides alone / The chief decides, and the city council has to agree / The chief decides, and the city manager has to agree

screens.why1: After who must agree comes what slows the buy, and for me that is the Axon bake-off, the RMS fit and the DA, so it lands right in the sales part of step 4.
screens.why2: Approvals, procurement and switching are the words every chief and city purchasing office uses, and the 25-word box is plain.
screens.why3: I sit through these trials, RMS integrations and prosecutor conversations with every agency, so I can answer from what I see each week.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a free-text answer.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my first item, the trial against Axon, but the 'about 8 weeks' is Keel's number, not one I typed, and 'or not need it' is awkward; it also drops the RMS check and the DA without saying they were set aside.
screens.instead: What could slow down or stop a purchase, and how long does it usually take? (e.g. a trial against Axon Draft One, an RMS fit check, the DA's sign-off; up to 25 words)

screens.why1: Straight after I named what could slow a purchase, this is where I check Keel's list of what has to happen first and which one the study tests.
screens.why2: The rows are in my trade's words (records system, prosecutor's office), but I'd say 'Draft One', not 'Axon's tool', and the belief's 'get through a side-by-side trial ... or not need it' takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know how my departments buy: the trial, the RMS check, the DA's office and the budget cycle are all things I see with chiefs every week.
screens.why4: 'A budget approval' overlaps the council and cap step I already set on the who-decides screens, and a CJIS or IT security review, a real gate for my buyers, is missing.
screens.why5: The trial, RMS and prosecutor rows are mine, but the added 'A budget approval' drifts from my point: at $30 per officer we sit under the chief's spending cap, so no council budget vote is needed.
screens.instead: What has to happen first: a 30-day trial against Draft One; a check it fits our RMS; a CJIS security sign-off; the DA's office accepting AI-drafted reports.

screens.why1: Right after I listed what could slow a purchase, picking the one to test and how long I expect it to take is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "If they bought it, how long would this step take before it went through" reads backwards for a trial that happens before the buy, and I had to read it twice to see it means how long until the deal closes.
screens.why3: I know these steps cold: Heber City ran 30 days with Draft One and 30 with us, so about 8 weeks is my own number.
screens.why4: The four steps are distinct and in my trade's words (records system, prosecutor's office, Axon's tool, budget approval), and the time box with days, weeks and months covers it.
screens.why5: The belief, a side-by-side trial against Axon's tool done within about 8 weeks or not needed, is what I picked and typed.
screens.instead: Intro: The chief gets one question about this step: from the day they start it, how long until it is done and they can sign. Pick the one step.

screens.why1: After who decides and what could stall a purchase, asking what first step I'd want a chief to take is the obvious last commercial question.
screens.why2: First real step is plain to me, and the hint (time, data, money or a signature) tells me a pilot that costs officers' time and footage counts.
screens.why3: Getting departments to run a pilot is exactly what I do every week, so I answer this from my own sales.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape chip, and leaving the commitment out is a sensible escape here.
screens.why5: The belief Keel wrote keeps my words, the chief running a free pilot with a few officers, and the added 'now' is harmless.

screens.why1: Right after I named my first step, Keel shows how that step reads to chiefs and what it will test, so I can check it before Part 3 goes out.
screens.why2: A free pilot with a few officers is exactly how chiefs and I talk about trying a tool, and the bar is stated plainly.
screens.why3: Whether a chief will take a free, no-strings pilot is the thing I deal with every week, and the Heber City and Wilton trials show chiefs do.
screens.why4: The bar of no more than 1 in 3 chiefs saying probably not or no fits a free pilot with no strings, and it counts 'probably not' as a no, which is the honest reading.
screens.why5: It keeps my step, but 'now' drifts from what I offer: I set up within 48 hours whenever they are ready, and a chief may still wait for the end of a budget cycle or for the prosecutor's office to sign off.
screens.instead: In most cases the police chief would let a few officers try it free for 30 days.

screens.why1: Right after I named my first step, a free pilot with a few officers, it makes sense to ask whether to collect sign-ups for it before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with "Yes, ask them" or "No pilot" is plain to me on first read; pilots are how I sell to departments.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call, and I do, since I fly out and set agencies up within 48 hours.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own decision.
screens.why5: The line drops my step's words, "a free pilot with a few officers", and doesn't say who gets it, yet a patrol officer can't sign the department up; only the chief can.
screens.instead: Ask the chiefs who say yes to leave an email for a free pilot with a few of their officers? (Yes, ask the chiefs / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking who asks the officers belongs at the last step before the study goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs in video, voice, typing, credits and text messages, and calls it a voice when the AI interviewer is also a face on video, so I'd read it twice to see what 400 credits buys me.
screens.why3: I know my officers and can judge which voice they'd sit through after a call, once I've played the two clips.
screens.why4: Two named voices with a 5-second clip each is a fair choice, but nothing says how Daphne and Saskia differ (tone, age, accent) for an audience of cops, and there's no text-only option for officers who won't talk to an AI on camera.
screens.why5: It asks about patrol officers, my own term, and nothing of Code Four's product or the chief's role leaks into it.
screens.instead: Who should ask patrol officers your questions? (Daphne — calm, plain-spoken ▶ / Saskia — brisk, direct ▶ / No voice — written questions only) · one recording for this project, 400 credits either way

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the patrol officers, it makes sense to set how the chiefs, who decide on the purchase, will answer their separate link.
screens.why2: The choice itself is clear, but the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' and the 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' status read like a glitch and need a second look.
screens.why3: As the founder I know chiefs are busy and would rather read and tap than sit for a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI video, read-and-tap, and let them choose are distinct and cover the real choices; nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my split between officers who use it and chiefs who pay, and nothing of the product leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should police chiefs answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them pick when they open the link

screens.why1: Choosing who gets the link belongs at the end, but the kicker already says SENT, and the screen does not say whether this is for the patrol officers or the chiefs I just set up on the screen before, which have to reach different people.
screens.why2: The three choices read easily, but "the Contacts page" names a part of Keel I have not seen on any earlier screen, so I would read that option twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would send this to: the chiefs and sergeants at our design-partner departments, and the officers they point me to.
screens.why4: The real route to patrol officers is missing: I ask a chief or sergeant to pass one link to their shift, which is not quite a named list and not a public post, and an officer on a department phone may not be able to sign in with Google.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but my answer of each person by name loses the two audiences, officers through Parts 1 and 2 and chiefs on Part 3, because the screen never says which link goes to whom.
screens.instead: Who gets the patrol officers' link, and who gets the chiefs' link? — People I know by name, each their own link / A chief or sergeant who passes one link to their officers / People I found with Keel / One open link posted where they already are

screens.why_b1: The verdict line says "Did not hold" and puts the deciding card and its number beside it (Purchase friction: 3 of 8 expect longer than 8 weeks), and the purchase-friction card shows the bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b2: Every card gives its count and its bar, but the denominators move between 8, 7 and 5 under a header that says 8 people answered: the 5 is explained (chiefs who would pay $30), the 7 on Existing sacrifice is not, so I had to look twice to see who was left out.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the exact lines I checked, word for word, and the other three cards are my own entry's beliefs in my own numbers ($30 per officer a month, 40 to 60 hours).
screens.why_b4: The only line under the verdict explains who was asked (chiefs, not patrol officers), and nothing says what a slow side-by-side trial against Axon means for me, such as timing pilots to the budget cycle or shortening the comparison.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, but the page never says 8 chiefs is a small sample: the stage fails on one chief over the bar, and three cards are called "Holding up" while sitting exactly at their bars (5 of 7, 4 of 5, 6 of 8).

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right beside the deciding count, 4 of 7 at 40 hours or more against a bar of 5 of 7 and 1 short, so I know it fell one chief short of holding and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts hours of incident reports per officer a month on a 0-to-80 axis over 7 chiefs, with the median at 40, my 40-to-60 band and the bar marker at 5 of 7, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Existing sacrifice' and 'Patrol officers already spend 40 to 60 hours a month on the incident reports' are my own figure and my own words.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and points to the Price card, but never says what a median sitting exactly on my low end means for the time-saved pitch or for the chiefs at 0, 20 and 30.
screens.why_b5: The low n is flagged ('a lean, not a call'), but Patricia's 'none' is counted as 0 hours of report writing, when a chief saying none most likely means the time is already paid for, and that answer tips the split against me.
screens.instead: Your median sits right on your low end, at 40 hours; pitch from 40, not 60. One 'none' probably means the time is already paid for, not zero hours, so treat this as a near-hold and ask the 20-to-30-hour chiefs how they counted.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 at $30 or more · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: The bands show how many chiefs fall in each, my $30 is marked at the low edge of its band, and the strip shows 5 for, 2 against with the marker at 5, all clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: Price, $30 per officer a month, is the figure and unit I named, and the belief line says it in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to Ability to pay, but it doesn't tell me whether to keep $30, raise it for the two chiefs at $50 or more, or what to do about the chief who won't spend on time already paid for.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (8 answered, 7 counted, Gerald set aside with the reason) and the count line itself says "a small group: a lean, not a call", so nothing claims more than seven chiefs can carry.
screens.instead: Holding exactly at the bar: one more chief under $30 and it fails; two would pay $50 or more after a pilot proves faster reports, so keep $30 as the entry price and answer the 'already paid time' objection with backlog and overtime.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 4 of 5 from money already there against a bar of 4 of 5, so I know it held, only just, and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: It plainly counts where the money would come from, over the 5 chiefs who named $30 or more, and the marker sits at 4 of 5 with the four for and one against shown at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The line uses my price and my buyer, the chief, so I recognise it, but Ability to pay was not one of the beliefs I checked on the way in; Keel wrote this one.
screens.why_b4: Sending me to the next card for who has to agree is useful, but the screen does not say what Marcus's new line means for me: a purchase over the chief's cap needs the council.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says this is a small group and a lean, but "expect the money to be there for the 5" overstates, since one of the 5 needs a new line signed off and 3 of the 8 chiefs never reached the question.
screens.instead: Just holding: 4 of the 5 chiefs who would pay $30 or more have a line for it already; Marcus would need a new line signed off, which is the council-approval risk to plan for; 3 of 8 never got this far.

screens.why_b1: The count '5 of 8 could sign alone · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short' sits beside the verdict, but 'People disagree' never says plainly that my belief did not hold, and its line names only 2 of the 3 against and drops the 'several people' answer.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see it counts chiefs by who signs off, over 8 chiefs, with my bar at 6, though the 'Yes' bar sitting between 'No' bars makes the for-versus-against split slightly slower to read.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Buyer and payer and carries the belief I checked word for word: 'The police chief decides, and nobody else has to agree.'
screens.why_b4: 'Expect someone else's agreement in some deals' is generic, even though the quotes right on the card name the council's budget approval and a city manager waiting on the DA, which tells me to have a council-and-DA packet ready for some deals.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it claims nothing beyond the 8 chiefs who answered.
screens.instead: Did not hold, 1 short: 5 of 8 chiefs could sign $30 per officer a month alone (bar 6). The other 3 need the council, the city manager, or someone else to decide, so for those deals plan for a budget-cycle approval and the DA's view on AI-drafted reports.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right above "3 of 8 expect longer than 8 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see the verdict and the one chief over the line at once.
screens.why_b2: Each band shows its count and whether it counts for or against me, 8 answered and 8 counted is stated, and the strip puts the bar at 6 of 8 with 5 for, so I can read what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits on first look.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and the line about a side-by-side trial against Axon's tool within about 8 weeks are exactly what I checked, though the bar line "You said a side-by-side trial against Axon's tool" tells me nothing new.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of that length" covers anything from 8 weeks to 6 months, which is too wide to plan a pilot or a sales cycle around, and it does not say whether to stretch the free trial or time it to the budget cycle.
screens.why_b5: The card says "a lean, not a call" and n stays visible, but it calls 8 weeks to 6 months "most often" when 1 month to under 8 weeks also has 3, so a tie is presented as the typical answer and the plan rests on it.
screens.instead: 3 of 8 chiefs expect the trial to run past 8 weeks, one over your bar; the answers split evenly, 3 at 1 month to under 8 weeks and 3 at 8 weeks to 6 months, so with 8 chiefs this is a lean. Check on the Insights tab whether the longer ones are waiting on the council or the budget cycle before you lengthen the free pilot.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the three answers to the pilot question over 8 chiefs, and the marker sits at 6 with the bar's rule spelt out (no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no), all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Commitment and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: the chief would run a free pilot with a few officers now.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is a concrete next step for me, and booking six pilots is exactly the 48-hour, no-strings setup I launched with.
screens.why_b5: n = 8 stays visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and a result exactly at the bar is called holding up rather than strong.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 would pilot, exactly at the bar, so one more no would flip it: book the six now, and ask Langford and Okonkwo what stops them.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word (People disagree, Did not hold, Holding up) with the deciding count and bar beside it, such as 3 of 8 expect longer than 8 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked: the chief decides alone, the side-by-side trial against Axon's tool within about 8 weeks, and $30 per officer a month.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do, so I have to work out the next step myself: line up the DA and city manager early, point to neighbouring departments, and offer a pilot that proves review times.
screens.why_b5: Every box keeps its n and its against count visible, says who never saw the why, and calls Price only 'at the bar' at 5 of 7, not strong.
screens.why_b6: Two things are new to me: chiefs wait on the district attorney's view and on what the sheriff's office next door decides, and one chief would pay more only after their own pilot shows faster reports that get through supervisor review.
screens.instead: Under Purchase friction, say why there are no voices (all 3 who were against were asked elsewhere). End with one line of next steps: bring the DA's and the neighbouring sheriff's view into the pilot offer, and make the pilot measure review pass-through.

screens.why1: On the chief's link, showing me the idea before asking what I'd pay for it is where it belongs, and as the first screen it frames everything after.
screens.why2: Records format, body-cam and redaction are my words, but 'check words they must catch' means nothing to me on first read, and calling Code Four 'a drafted narrative report' made me stop, since it's a tool, not a report.
screens.why3: My officers write these reports off body-cam every shift, so I can weigh this from what my department actually does.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It drifts: the first line names the product as a report rather than a tool that drafts one, and the belief says 'you' review and sign when it's my officers who would, with 'check words' reading like the builder's own term.
screens.why6: The sentences are short, but heard once the opener sounds wrong, 'check words they must catch' won't land by ear, and the whole card runs long to hold in one listening.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts police reports from body-cam footage. Your officers upload a call's footage, and it drafts the narrative in your records format, with each fact tied to its clip and planted errors they must catch before they sign. It also redacts footage and searches across it. The people building it believe your officers would review and sign a draft instead of writing from scratch.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what report writing costs my officers in time is the obvious place to start on the buying side.
screens.why2: I'd say 'my officers' or 'the department', not 'your team', and 'hours per officer' makes me average across my whole roster in my head before I can answer.
screens.why3: As chief I know report writing eats patrol time, but I don't track hours per officer per month, so I'd be guessing off a sergeant's complaint or a rough shift estimate.
screens.why4: The number box is fine, but there are two escapes where there should be one, and 'None' is a near-useless chip since no department of mine spends zero hours on reports.
screens.why5: It still asks about writing up reports, but it moved from the founder's last 7 days to last month and dropped the body-cam footage-to-report part, so it reads as all paperwork rather than the after-call write-up.
screens.why6: The stem says fine, but 'or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clipped instruction that's hard to follow by ear and sounds like a second escape.
screens.instead: Think of your patrol officers last week: about how many hours did each spend writing up reports from calls with body-cam footage? (number of hours; or say I can't recall)

screens.why1: Right after asking how many hours my officers spend on reports, asking what the tool is worth per officer per month is the obvious next step for the guy who signs the check.
screens.why2: Per officer, per month is exactly how body-cam, records and report-writing vendors quote me, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I set the budget and buy per-seat software for my department, so I know what I would pay per officer.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct, cover the range from cheap to premium seat pricing, include a will-not-pay floor, and the one escape fits.
screens.why5: The card calls Code Four a drafted narrative report rather than a tool that drafts the report from body-cam footage, so the idea has drifted a little.
screens.why6: The two-step bands say well, but the escape comes out as or say you can't say, which is clumsy when heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine Code Four, a tool that drafts the incident report from body-cam footage. What would it be worth to you a month, per officer? Under $10 / $10 to under $30 / $30 to under $50 / $50 to under $100 / $100 or more / I wouldn't pay for this; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I named a monthly price per officer, asking where that money would come from is the natural next step for me as the chief who pays.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are how I talk about my own department budget, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: Where the money comes from is my job: my budget, my council and my grants.
screens.why4: The options switch to past tense ('we already had', 'there was no budget') for a what-if, and grant or forfeiture money, a common way small departments pay for tech, has no place of its own.
screens.why5: Only Code Four's name and my own price came back to me, with no founder terms leaking.
screens.why6: The four options say well as a list, but the closing 'Or say you can't say' is clumsy to hear.
screens.instead: You said about $30 to $50 a month. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have · A new line the council or manager approves · A grant or forfeiture funds · Cut from other spending · There'd be no money for it — or: I can't say

screens.why1: Right after where the money would come from, it's natural to ask whether I can approve the spend myself or have to take it to the city manager or council.
screens.why2: Plain enough, but I think about signing authority as a total contract amount against my purchasing limit, not a per-officer monthly figure, so I'd have to do the math across my roster first.
screens.why3: I know my approval limits cold, but whether $30 per officer clears them depends on headcount and term, so the honest answer is 'depends on the total', and I'd half guess.
screens.why4: 'Someone else would have to agree' and 'it would be someone else's decision' blur together, three of four options start with 'No' with Yes buried second, and the common chief answer, 'within my budget, but council over a threshold', has no clean home.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or the founder's roles shows here; it's a plain approval question about a price I gave.
screens.why6: Three spoken options starting 'no, ... someone' are hard to keep apart by ear, and 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy aloud.
screens.instead: At about $30 per officer a month for your whole department, who would have to approve it? I could approve it from my budget; I'd need the city manager or administrator; it would have to go to council or the board; or it's not my decision at all. (escape: I can't say)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off on the money, it makes sense to ask how long the trial step would hold the purchase up.
screens.why2: I know what a side-by-side trial against Axon's Draft One means, but a trial doesn't 'go through' — a purchase does — so I'd read the stem twice to work out whether it means how long the trial runs or how long until we could buy.
screens.why3: I can judge how long a pilot would run here, but it assumes we're on Axon's report tool; if we only have their cameras, or another vendor's, I'd be guessing what we'd test against.
screens.why4: The bands cover the range, but '1 month to under 8 weeks' mixes months and weeks so it reads like a typo, and 'Over 1 year' is a band I'd never see for a 30-day pilot.
screens.why5: The trial against Axon's tool comes through as the step the founder meant, but 'before it went through' drifts off it, and naming Axon as the incumbent puts the founder's view of my shop in front of me.
screens.why6: Four options said first is easy to hold, but the stem runs past twenty words with an awkward ending, and 'one month to under eight weeks' is a mouthful heard aloud.
screens.instead: If you bought Code Four, how long would you want to test it against Axon's Draft One before buying? Under a month · 1 to 2 months · 2 to 6 months · Over 6 months · We wouldn't need a test — or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: After price, budget, sign-off and the trial question, asking whether I'd actually put a few of my officers on a free pilot is the natural last step.
screens.why2: A free pilot with a few officers is exactly how I'd talk about trying report software, so I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: Whether to let a handful of my patrol officers try a tool is my call, so I know my answer.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided, with one yes and two shades of no, so there's no 'probably' on the yes side, which is where I'd land until I know it works with our Axon footage and our records system.
